articles.summary: COVID, global warming, conspiracy theorists, natural disasters, financial collapses – and a sham social media ban. It’s no wonder young Australians are glum.

articles.title: India, UK Fire Up Defense Cooperation With Joint Development
articles.full_text:
An inter-governmental agreement to develop and incorporate integrated full electric propulsion for the Indian Navy’s four landing platform docks is underway.
India’s Defense Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh shakes hands with U.K.’s Permanent Under Secretary for Defense Jeremy Pocklington at the 25th India–UK Defense Consultative Group Meeting at New Delhi, India, on August 21, 2026.
India and the United Kingdom are close to signing two inter-governmental agreements (IGAs) for the incorporation of electric propulsion on Indian Navy ships and production of Marlet lightweight multirole missiles (LMM). These are decisive steps toward forging long-term defense industrial cooperation and deepening the bilateral strategic partnership.
At the same time, the U.K. has also upped its pitch for another mega-deal — the design and development of a jet engine to power the advanced medium combat aircraft (AMCA), India’s fifth-generation fighter.
The two countries have made concerted efforts to deepen defense cooperation and find a long-term overarching deal to anchor that effort. This intent was formalized in the 10‑year Defense Industrial Roadmap under the “Vision 2035” announced last year, which focuses on deepening collaboration in advanced technologies and complex weapons, supporting innovation and co-development, through cooperation programs such as the Jet Engine Advanced Core Technologies. It also calls for strengthening research and development on developing new capabilities, including underwater systems and direct energy weapons.
The expanding military-to-military cooperation, joint exercises and research collaborations add to the broadening cooperation. Another important binding factor is overlapping concerns and converging interests in the Indo-Pacific, where Britain sees India as one of the most important “stabilizing forces.”
Beyond defense and security, the overall relationship too has leapfrogged with high-level commitment from both sides. That push led to the conclusion of the bilateral Free Trade Agreement (FTA), one of the biggest trade deals of modern times, that came into effect on July 15, 2026.
Integrated Full Electric Propulsion (IFEP)
The IGA to be signed is to develop and incorporate IFEP for the Indian Navy’s four landing platform docks (LPD) for which a separate tender is underway. The conversation for deploying IFEP on Indian Navy’s future vessels is several years old, as the Indian Navy set its sights on shifting from diesel to electric propulsion engines to bring in efficiency, and reduce fossil fuel dependency and emissions.
Formalizing the conversation, a joint working group called the “India-UK electric propulsion capability partnership” was set up in early 2023. A Statement of Intent to co-design, co-create and co-produce maritime electric propulsion systems was signed in November 2024, and the intent to finalize an IGA was announced when the India and British prime ministers met in Mumbai in October 2025. As part of the cooperation, GE Vernova and state-owned Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited announced the setting up of India’s first land-based test facility for IFEP.
However, IFEP systems on four LPDs are just the start, as the Indian Navy is targeting a 200-ship force by 2035 in response to expanding Chinese naval numbers and presence in the Indian Ocean Region. Some existing ships could also be converted to electric propulsion. The IFEP brings significant operational efficiencies in this regard, which the Royal Navy has mastered, having operationally deployed it on several frontline ships, including its aircraft carrier. In April 2023, U.K.’s Chief of Defense Staff Admiral Sir Tony Radakin observed that the U.K. is one of the world’s leaders in maritime electric propulsion, having been on it for at least 20 years, and cooperation with the U.K. means that India “doesn’t have to go through a 20-year journey.”
The LPD project, an ambition for almost two decades, received a fresh sanction from the Defense Acquisition Council, the highest body for procurements in India’s Ministry of Defense, in October 2025. These vessels, displacing around 29,000 tons, will be built by Indian shipyards in partnership with foreign partners.
Once rolled out, this deal will intertwine collaboration over the next several decades. However, given India’s notorious procurement process, the IFEP deployment depends on the LPD deal reaching its logical conclusion in a reasonable timeframe.
India is looking for a global partner for design and development of a 120kN jet engine to power the AMCA-Mk2. While negotiations between Safran of France and Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE) have been ongoing for several years now, the delay opened prospects for the U.K’s Rolls Royce and the U.S.’ General Electric. Rolls Royce, which has been working closely with the Indian research establishment for several years, has presented a compelling offer, including full control over Intellectual Property for the engine developed.
On August 14, Rolls Royce announced a partnership with Reliance Industries Limited to explore the formation of a dedicated Aerospace Gas Turbine Complex that will be a center of excellence for power and propulsion technology in India. This significantly ups the ante in support of its offer.
However, some practical realities stand out, which will determine partner selection. For instance, despite assurance that U.S. International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) does not apply to engine collaboration as it’s an IGA, concerns remain in Indian policy circles given Britain’s alliance with the U.S. and possible impact on future deals.
This is particularly so as all the variants of India’s indigenous light combat aircraft and AMCA-Mk1, cumulatively about half the fighter squadron strength in two decades, will be powered by GE engines, a U.S. company. That positions France favorably given its independent arms industry and the trajectory of Indo-French ties. Adding to that is India’s interest in joining the French future combat air system (FCAS), sixth-generation fighter program. If the same engine or its derivative can go into the FCAS, that would be a lucrative proposition both economically and operationally.
Last year, India and the U.K. made several important announcements on the defense front. At Aero India in February 2025, U.K. announced the formal launch of “Defense Partnership–India,” or DP-I, a dedicated cell within the U.K. Ministry of Defense for deepening cooperation.
Several cooperation agreements were also signed at the biennial expo in Bengaluru, including production of Starstreak man portable air defense systems (MANPADS) and LMMs and the establishment of an advanced short-range air to air missile (ASRAAM) assembly and test facility in India.
The two countries also conducted their largest-ever maritime exercise last year that saw their Carrier Strike Groups exercise together. A separate air defense exercise saw the Royal Navy deploying its aircraft to exercise with the Indian Navy and Indian Air Force.
A contract for laser beam riding Starstreak Man-portable air-defense systems or MANPADS was also signed between Thales U.K. and Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) under the Emergency Procurement route for 16 launchers, 56 missiles and one simulator worth around $35 million. This could potentially expand to thousands of missiles in future. The two companies had then announced their intent for collaboration to produce LMMs in India. The IGA to be signed soon will make India one of the largest markets for the missiles. Similarly, weapons manufacturer MBDA U.K. and BDL are setting up a first-of-its-kind ASRAAM assembly and test facility in Hyderabad to also cater to exports, after the missile was chosen for the Jaguar and Light Combat Aircraft-Mk1A.
British defense companies like Thales, Rolls Royce and several others have integrated Indian companies into their global supply chains. With the expanding cooperation and an enabling FTA, this is set to significantly expand. With the Indian defense manufacturing ecosystem significantly maturing over the years, it offers scale and capacity, the criticality of which was showcased in the West Asia conflict.
Military-to-military engagements have also expanded. For instance, with agreement early this year on the deployment of three IAF qualified flying instructors to a Royal Air Force training base, Indian officers are now embedded as instructors at all three UK service academies. Britain has also been leveraging the bilateral logistics sharing agreement signed in 2022 to augment its deployments in the Indian Ocean Region. In addition to spares and supplies, under the logistics pact, Royal Navy ships have undergone essential repair at an Indian shipyard during their deployment in the region. Britain was the fifth country to post a liaison officer at the Indian Navy’s Information Fusion Centre for Indian Ocean Region (IFC-IOR) in Gurugram inaugurated in 2018 to promote maritime domain awareness.
The India-U.K. relationship has struggled with several irritants in the past, including Khalistani separatism in the U.K, and Britain’s ties with Pakistan. However, there is determination on both sides to expand ties amid geopolitical uncertainties and a changing world order.
With this slew of agreements, Britain is looking to regain lost space in India’s growing defense sector. For India, the U.K is one of the important stabilizing vectors in its multilateral alignment strategy to safeguard its interests.

articles.title: Japan’s Record 2027 Defense Budget Request Is Only the Opening Bid
articles.full_text:
Tokyo is building a force around AI, unmanned systems, a high-low weapons mix, and greater staying power.
The destroyer JS Kaga, the second ship of the Izumo class.
Japan’s Ministry of Defense on August 31 submitted a record fiscal year 2027 budget request of roughly 8.9 trillion yen ($55.5 billion). But the headline figure tells only part of the story.
At a media briefing three days before the announcement, Defense Ministry officials said around 160 entries in the request were marked as “item requests” (jiko yokyu), for which no specific funding amount has yet been assigned. The reason is that Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s government plans to revise Japan’s three key security documents – the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy, and Defense Buildup Program – by the end of 2026. Even procurement quantities for some major equipment could change as part of that review.
The 8.9 trillion yen figure should therefore be seen less as a final price tag than as an opening bid. The budget request will be sent to the Finance Ministry for consideration before a decision is made in late December. The fiscal 2027 budget is set to mark a 15th consecutive annual increase and a 13th consecutive record high, with the final figure widely expected to exceed 10 trillion yen for the first time.
Fiscal year (FY) 2027 is the final year of Japan’s current five-year Defense Buildup Program, which set total defense spending at roughly 43 trillion yen from FY2023 through 2027. But ministry officials said the security environment has changed with greater speed and complexity than anticipated when the current documents were drafted. The request is therefore not simply about completing the existing buildup. It is a bridge to the next phase of Japan’s defense transformation.
The ministry organized the request around three main pillars and nine priority areas. The first, adapting to “new ways of warfare,” covers AI, unmanned systems, stand-off capabilities, integrated air and missile defense, space, and cyber. The second focuses on sustained response capabilities, including Pacific and sea-lane defense, while the third centers on the foundations of defense, including the defense industrial and technological base and personnel.
Artificial intelligence and unmanned systems are central to that transformation. The ministry plans an AI-based decision-support system for the Self-Defense Forces’ (SDF) Joint Operations Command, together with a next-generation AI platform and secure cloud infrastructure. The request also includes UAVs for intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeting, attack UAVs, small unmanned ground vehicles, and research into a stand-off missile launch module for unmanned underwater vehicles.
Another major investment is Japan’s next-generation fighter, which is being jointly developed with the United Kingdom and Italy under the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP). The ministry’s Acquisition, Technology, and Logistics Agency (ATLA) requested 234 billion yen ($1.5 billion), plus an item request, to push ahead with the fighter program. The funding will support Japan’s contribution to the GCAP International Government Organization (GIGO), joint design work, and the maturation of technologies Japan is developing independently.
ATLA also requested 9.7 billion yen ($61 million), plus an item request, to accelerate research and development of collaborative unmanned aircraft equipped with deception and electronic warfare capabilities and capable of autonomous decision-making while operating alongside the next-generation fighter.
The emphasis on cost and quantity is particularly evident in Japan’s expanding stand-off capabilities. Alongside sophisticated domestically developed missiles, the ministry plans to develop lower-cost stand-off missiles at home while acquiring foreign-made weapons to obtain the capability more quickly. Officials cited U.S. defense company Anduril Industries’ Barracuda as one system under consideration for a concept involving lower-cost stand-off weapons released from transport aircraft.
In effect, the concept amounts to a high-low mix. Lower-cost weapons could complement more sophisticated missiles, allowing Japan to field greater numbers of weapons, while transport aircraft would diversify its launch platforms.
The ministry also plans to begin development of an underwater-launched hypersonic guided missile, exploiting the greater survivability of underwater platforms.
A similar cost-exchange problem is shaping Japan’s defenses. The ministry plans to develop a Ground Self-Defense Force Close-Range Air Defense System, or CRADS, combining guided missiles, an autocannon, and lasers to counter various airborne threats, including low-cost drones that can be fielded in large numbers. Japan is separately pursuing high-power microwave technology against UAVs and expanding the use of decoys.
The underlying lesson is that quantity matters again. Japan is moving toward a mix of high-end and lower-cost systems on both sides of the offense-defense equation.
Staying power runs through the request as well. With Russia’s invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year, the ministry argues that the ability to sustain a prolonged conflict is itself important for deterrence. The request places greater emphasis on ammunition and guided missiles, fuel, food, transportation, and logistics, while also studying the introduction of transport vessels equipped with autonomous navigation technologies.
Against the backdrop of increased Chinese carrier operations in the Pacific and flights by Chinese and Russian bombers, Japan is also placing new emphasis on Pacific sea-lane defense. The ministry requested 292.2 billion yen ($1.8 billion), plus an item request, to acquire 17 MQ-9B SeaGuardian UAVs. The request also includes further modifications to the Izumo-class destroyers, surveillance facilities on Kitadaito Island in Okinawa Prefecture, and a study of cargo-handling facilities on Iwo To to improve maritime transport.
The ministry sums up its approach to the defense industrial base with a striking phrase: “production capacity itself is deterrence.” The government plans to strengthen domestic production and technology, promote equipment transfers and innovation, and establish a new government-backed organization to reinforce the defense industrial base.
The challenge is financial as much as technological. Officials said the request was calculated at 149 yen to the dollar, compared with the 108 yen benchmark used when the current five-year buildup plan was drawn up in 2022. They acknowledged that the weaker yen has raised the cost of imported equipment and foreign-made components, eroding Japan’s purchasing power.
Taken together, the FY2027 request points toward an SDF that will be more unmanned, more networked, more reliant on stand-off weapons, better prepared for mass attacks, and more closely supported by Japan’s industrial base. But with around 160 entries still unpriced – including programs central to Japan’s future defense posture – the biggest question remains unanswered: How much will this transformation actually cost?

articles.title: After 25 Years, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Faces an Uncertain Future
articles.full_text:
The SCO faces an uncertain future. Its key members fear each other at least as much as they need each other.
Family photos during the 2025 SCO Summit in Tianjin, China, Sep. 1, 2025.
The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit, taking place on August 31 and September 1, will be another opportunity for China and Russia to try to promote an alternative to Western-led international institutions. But the organization, now in its 25th year, faces internal rivalries and tensions that are becoming ever more difficult to sweep under the rug.
The SCO appears to be high on geopolitical symbolism and low on genuine relevance, at least on the political and security front. Despite its Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS) and the Peace Mission military exercises between SCO member countries, the organization’s security agenda has been weak, with very little to show in terms of actual results. It is not a security treaty, and it has had little effect in diluting the political and military tension between its major players.
One such point of tension is the Sino-Indian conflict. This is a long-running contest that predates the SCO by decades and periodically erupts into clashes at their disputed border. The most recent one took place in 2020 and was unusually violent, causing the first casualties resulting from such clashes in decades and throwing the relationship into a freezer. Talks this month have made some progress, but the fundamentals of the border conflict are likely to remain unresolved. The two sides have discussed ways to improve understanding of the border demarcation in appropriate areas. In an effort to manage border issues, two new additional military hotlines were agreed upon to connect India’s Eastern Army Command and Central Army Command with their Chinese counterparts. While these institutionalized communication channels are useful to avoid incidents along parts of border, an absence of mechanisms is not necessarily the problem. These may be useful, though in previous crises, such mechanisms were not.
A larger problem is that China’s growth and power have created new security complications for countries such as India, which is carefully managing its engagements with the SCO as a fine diplomatic balancing act between Washington on one side and Beijing and Moscow on the other. While its relationship with Washington has come under stress, New Delhi understands the limits of alternative options. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s engagements with the SCO, the Quad, and other minilateral groupings are a demonstration of what India calls its multidirectional foreign policy. A good example of this emerged from the 2025 SCO Summit in Tianjin, where a photo op between Modi, China’s Xi Jinping, and Russia’s Vladimir Putin gave India an opportunity to show that it had options. However, the fact that China continues to be India’s most important national security threat will limit the utility of these partnerships. The SCO cannot resolve these problems.
Still, in 25 years, the SCO has evolved from having a narrow Central Asia border security focus to become a wider regional institution. Beijing and Moscow’s use of the SCO to speak the language of multipolarity has found certain appeal among Global South countries seeking alternatives to Western-led architectures. But this message is clouded as the two repeatedly violate the U.N. Charter by taking unilateral actions against their neighbors, exhibiting little respect for international law. Many in the Global South may ignore such violations, but the hypocrisy tends to accumulate and undermine the legitimacy of such messaging. Moreover, countries such as India don’t want the SCO to become such an anti-Western grouping.
One area where the SCO is progressing is in intra-group trade, though it’s unclear if the organization itself was responsible for this. This is also primarily driven by China-Russia and China-India bilateral trade. By some estimates, intra-SCO trade in 2024 was worth $725 billion , up from $463 billion in 2021. The initiative to establish an SCO Development Bank, which the members agreed to in principle at the 2025 Summit, would further strengthen Beijing’s efforts to shape a new economic architecture, potentially as “China’s answer to Western financial hegemony.” China has been pushing this since 2010 with the goal of expanding the global footprint of the Chinese yuan and emerging as an alternative to Western-led post-Bretton Wood institutions.
But even here, there are problems. The SCO Bank initiative itself is not without its frictions and fears. Russia is a reluctant supporter because of Moscow’s fear of Chinese economic dominance in Central Asia, traditionally Russia’s backyard. India has also remained skeptical of the bank because it would enhance China’s regional dominance. In fact, this has been an issue since the SCO began. While China wanted it to be a regional economic grouping, Russia made every effort to shape it as a security bloc precisely due to a fear of Chinese dominance. Furthermore, India works closely with Western financial institutions and is against the idea of making the SCO into an anti-Western bloc driven by China and Russia.
The SCO faces an uncertain future. Its key members fear each other at least as much as they need each other, and the reasons they need each other are themselves varied. There is no acknowledged leader to the group either, despite China’s material dominance. This isn’t a solid foundation for any ambitious structure, but it may survive because none of the major partners can afford to abandon it.

articles.title: Why South Asia’s Governments Must Build Disaster Institutions That Reflect the Region’s Borderless Hazards
articles.full_text:
A glacier fell across the China-Nepal border. The flood crossed three countries. But South Asian countries’ responses to natural disasters are limited by borders and politics.
A consignment of medicines, food packets and other supplies being loaded onto an aircraft that India dispatched as part of its humanitarian support to Nepalis impacted by the August 26 floods in Nepal, August 27, 2028.
When part of a glacier collapsed above the Lhende Khola on August 26, the debris flow it triggered was initially mistaken by the U.S. Geological Survey’s automated network for a magnitude-4.4 earthquake. By August 30, the combined toll in Nepal and China’s Tibet had reached around 750 dead, with more than 3,000 missing, including nearly 900 hydropower workers feared trapped.
Nepal’s finance minister estimates rebuilding will cost $4-5 billion, nearly a tenth of the Nepali economy. The collapse occurred on the Nepali side, on Langtang Lirung, which lies wholly within Nepal, but the debris fell into the Lhende Khola-Donglin Tsangpo river system, which crosses the Nepal-China border. The flood surged through Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, while rising downstream levels prompted precautionary evacuations in parts of India. The hazards crossed borders. The mechanisms for responding to them have remained largely national.
South Asia’s problem is not a shortage of frameworks to deal with natural disasters. After the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, SAARC’s 2005 Dhaka Declaration called for a permanent regional mechanism for disaster preparedness, relief and rehabilitation. A 2006 Comprehensive Framework promised shared early-warning and cross-border data exchange. A Rapid Response mechanism agreed after Pakistan’s 2010 floods entered into force only in 2016, and many provisions have struggled to acquire operational continuity. SAARC’s non-functioning has further hindered a regional response; the grouping has not held a summit since 2014. India, Bangladesh and BIMSTEC have developed bilateral and subregional mechanisms because SAARC has been non-functional for a decade. But even these working instruments remain disconnected.
Disaster cooperation has four parts: monitoring, data-sharing, warning and response. Monitoring tells us what is happening upstream; data-sharing determines who learns about it and how quickly; warning tells downstream governments and populations what to do; response determines whether teams and equipment can cross a border. South Asia has instruments for each, but lacks the chain connecting them.
The 2008 Kosi flood showed the cost of that missing chain. When the eastern Kosi embankment breached at Kushaha in Nepal, some 50,000 Nepalis and millions in Bihar in India were affected. A World Bank assessment recorded 3.3 million affected and nearly 500 deaths. Water scholar Ajaya Dixit identified a core institutional gap: the 1966 Kosi treaty did not establish a clearly defined bilateral operational channel for embankment monitoring and maintenance. That did not cause the breach, but left no fast mechanism to turn warning into downstream evacuation. In 2017, floods across India, Nepal and Bangladesh affected an estimated 41 million people, yet the response remained largely national.
The 2023 South Lhonak glacial lake outburst in Sikkim made the same point. Researchers had estimated a 42 percent probability of the lake bursting. It sent a 20-meter wave through the Teesta-III dam and 385 kilometers into Bangladesh. India’s forecasters alerted Bangladesh the same day, but the lake’s early-warning system was still being installed — a year late. This was initially a failure of domestic preparedness, not a cross-border cooperation failure.
But that domestic lapse does not stand apart from the region’s wider pattern. The weakness exists at every layer, from monitoring to data exchange, warning and response. Foreknowledge is not the missing ingredient.
The response to last week’s glacier collapse and flooding in the Tibet-Nepal region follows a familiar pattern. China’s Premier Li Qiang travelled to the affected Gyirong sector within a day, while India sent relief flights and medical teams within 48 hours. Kathmandu initially declined foreign teams, but later accepted limited foreign expertise for tunnel rescue, DNA testing and forensic work after international pressure. India has offered assistance for Nepal to take up as it sees fit. The aid is generous, but negotiated afresh rather than activated through a standing protocol.
Nepal’s consent matters, particularly for security-linked deployments, but the question is whether technical assistance can be pre-negotiated so tunnelling teams, DNA units and bridging equipment activate in hours rather than days.
India and Bangladesh’s Joint Rivers Commission offers a working model. Since 1972, it has shared water-level, discharge and rainfall data on major rivers, with the annual sharing window extended in 2022. Bangladeshi officials say it falls short of real-time forecasting on smaller rivers. The 1996 Ganges Water Sharing Treaty expires in December 2026; formal renewal talks have not begun, despite an Indian parliamentary panel urging action.
BIMSTEC offers experience that South Asia can draw on. India has hosted Disaster Management Exercises since 2017, including rounds in 2020, 2021 and 2025. Yet when a magnitude-7.7 earthquake struck Myanmar in March 2025, it did not produce a comparable regional deployment. Instead, India launched Operation Brahma, reaching the ground within a day. A BIMSTEC Centre of Excellence for Disaster Management was proposed weeks later. The bloc is rehearsing interoperability faster than it is institutionalizing it.
The most difficult test is managing cooperation with China. India and China have an Expert-Level Mechanism on trans-border rivers, established in 2006 for annual meetings and flood-season data exchange. But its continuity is fragile. The Sutlej hydrological-data MoU expired in November 2020 and the Brahmaputra MoU in June 2023. China suspended Brahmaputra data-sharing during the 2017 Doklam standoff, citing damage to hydrological stations.

Such arrangements can also be affected by the wider state of bilateral relations, making continuity an institutional vulnerability. China had also said a year earlier it would use the mechanism and share hydrological data during emergencies on humanitarian grounds.

Former Nepali Environment Minister Madhav Prasad Chaulagain recently said that Nepal received no timely warning from China before the August 26 disaster; a protocol agreed after a smaller 2025 glacier incident was not used. What it has not built is the chain that turns that knowledge into a warning someone downstream can act on, or into a response that can cross a border when minutes matter.

articles.title: Sri Lanka’s New Anti-Terrorism Legislation
articles.full_text:
A law that cannot turn intelligence into evidence will reproduce the central weakness of the Prevention of Terrorism Act of 1979, regardless of how much power it gives the state.
Sri Lanka’s Cabinet has approved a bill to replace the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) of 1979. The official Cabinet decision calls the replacement the “Safeguarding the State from Terrorism” Bill, while the government’s December 2025 consultation draft uses the term “Protection of the State from Terrorism.”
The National People’s Power (NPP) government has not given any reason yet for the change of name of the proposed legislation. It will be published in the Gazette and then presented to Parliament.
The Cabinet-approved text has not yet been made public. The only version that can presently be examined is the 2025 December draft, but it is unlikely that the bill will be significantly different from the draft, given the extensive consultations that followed the December draft.
The 2025 December draft is an improvement over the PTA of 1979. It attempts to define terrorism and related preparatory offenses more narrowly than the PTA did. It also contains safeguards that were absent or weaker under the PTA. For example, the draft recognizes access to counsel, requires notification of detention, provides for magistrates and the Human Rights Commission to visit detention facilities, and requires a detainee held under a detention order to be produced before a magistrate every 14 days. It restricts the use of statements made in custody — an important departure from the PTA’s admission of confessions made to senior police officers. A February 2026 assessment by United Nations experts acknowledged these improvements.
However, the December 2025 draft does not curb the exceptional executive power that critics of the PTA want. Under the December draft, the defense secretary can still renew two-month detention orders for a year. When a detention order is produced, the magistrate is expected to approve it, rather than decide independently whether the evidence justifies continued custody. The president may proscribe organizations and impose curfews, while the armed forces and Coast Guard receive powers normally associated with the police.
The government has not explained why it chose “Safeguarding the State from Terrorism,” as a title for the proposed law. But a law framed around safeguarding “the state” probably looks at protecting aspects such as sovereignty, territorial integrity, government institutions, and public order.
Sri Lanka has legitimate security interests and needs counterterror laws. It fought the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) for decades. At one point, the LTTE controlled about one-third of Sri Lanka’s territory.  More recently, the 2019 Easter Sunday attackers targeted civilians and hotels, killing 269 people. But the attack also challenged the state’s capacity to detect and deter transnational ideological threats.
The December draft brings all these interests together. Some of its provisions criminalize the collection or supply of broadly defined “confidential information” that may affect national security and defense. Executive proscription, curfew, and the power the police still wields reinforce the state-security character of the law.
Cabinet spokesman Nalinda Jayatissa said the bill would cover terrorism “including organized crimes.” If that formulation appears in the final text, Parliament should ask whether the law is defining a distinct offense or simply extending counterterrorism powers to difficult forms of ordinary crime.
Sri Lanka nevertheless needs a preventive counterterrorism capacity. The Penal Code can punish crime like murder after the act. But terrorist attacks must be interrupted earlier. The state must act when would-be perpetrators are financing an operation, acquiring weapons, training recruits, selecting targets, or coordinating across borders.
These needs have grown more complex since 1979, when Sri Lanka enacted its first anti-terrorism law amid the looming threat posed by the LTTE. For example, the internet allows small groups to access information and technical knowledge from like-minded individuals based abroad. Terrorist financing can move through digital assets today and is better hidden than in the past.
The December draft recognizes some of this change. It reaches preparatory conduct, financing, transnational activity, and digital communications. It provides judicial authorization for interception and compelled decryption. These focus more on disruption than after-the-fact arrest and confession.
Custody still remains the main debating point of anti-terrorism legislation in the country. Counterterrorism investigations take time, and the complexity of these operations justify more investigative time. However, prolonged custody does not automatically lead to success against terrorism.
The PTA was fully operational when suicide bombers in 2019 killed more than 260 people.  A parliamentary investigation and the presidential commission of inquiry found that officials had received specific warnings but failed to evaluate, share, and act on them. The state possessed extensive arrest and detention powers. What it lacked was institutional capacity to disrupt the attacks.
However, the 2025 December draft does not establish how intelligence agencies should share information, how competing warnings should be assessed, who is responsible for acting on them, or how intelligence should be converted into evidence that can survive trial. Those are matters of institutional design, resources and accountability as much as law.
One improvement over the 1979 law that the 2025 draft provides for is limiting the use of confessions made to the police as evidence. The question is whether the final bill creates conditions for financial, communications, and forensic evidence to replace confession-centered investigations, or merely adds safeguards around the old model.
The bill should therefore be judged by whether it is somewhat more liberal than the PTA. Once the Cabinet-approved text is gazetted, three questions will matter. Has the definition separated terrorist violence from protest, organized crime, and political advocacy? Can a court examine the basis for continued detention rather than simply record an executive decision? And does the law help institutions convert intelligence into timely disruption and prosecutable evidence?
Sri Lanka’s history shows why preventive powers are necessary. It also shows that locking people up for extended periods is not the same as prevention. A law designed to safeguard the state should strengthen the state’s ability to recognize and stop a credible threat.
The NPP government has an opportunity to move Sri Lanka away from a system that measures security through arrests and years spent in custody. The better test is whether the law helps the authorities disrupt credible threats and build cases that survive in court. A law that cannot turn intelligence into evidence will reproduce the central weakness of the PTA, regardless of how much power it gives the state.

articles.title: India Has a Complex Youth Unemployment Problem, And There Isn’t a Quick Fix
articles.full_text:
Education and skills don’t match available jobs. The economy isn’t creating good-quality employment for an expanding and increasingly educated workforce.
India has been struggling with a multi-faceted employment problem, which is triggering deep frustration among its youth, especially those who are educated.
This frustration was on display recently, when tens of thousands of young women and men protested at New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. While the immediate trigger for the protests was leaked question papers for medical entrance examinations, the underlying cause is frustration with an education system that doesn’t lead to meaningful employment.
The Indian economy is among the world’s fastest-growing large economies. Yet, it is producing an ever-increasing number of educated unemployed youth.
The problems are multifold. First, India is struggling to connect education and skills with available jobs. Second, its economy is not creating good-quality employment for a rapidly expanding and increasingly educated workforce. And third, poor government recruitment has rendered generic university degrees largely useless.
The warnings have been there for quite some time. A 2018 article by Indrajit Bairagya in the Economic and Political Weekly noted that the unemployment rate among the educated is not only higher than that among the uneducated, but it also increases with higher levels of education. Youth, both educated and uneducated, are more likely to be unemployed than older people. One reason is that the educated are unwilling to take low-grade informal jobs, while sufficient regular salaried jobs are also not available.
Developments over the last few years reveal a deeply worrying situation. A recent report titled “Reimagining Skilling for Viksit Bharat@2047,” published by NITI Aayog, the top policy advisor to the government of India, in August this year, said only 8.25 percent of graduates are employed in roles aligned with their qualifications. The remaining 91.75 percent are not working in roles that use the qualifications they acquired. They either acquired additional skills or are working below their skill level, the report said, blaming the poor education-to-job transition rate for India’s growing youth unemployment.
The report says that 80 percent of higher education students identify inadequate practical experience and industry exposure as a major problem. Degrees, diplomas and certificates do not consistently translate into employability when curricula remain disconnected from evolving workplace requirements. As a result, the unemployment rate among graduates stood at 13 percent, compared with the national unemployment rate of 3.2 percent; among women graduates, it was 20.4 percent.
The NITI report reveals that generic degrees don’t provide a direct pathway to employment. When a student with a graduate degree fails to land a job, she either turns to additional degrees or invests in coaching classes that she hopes will lead to a job. All these enhance the overall education costs for improving employability. The cost burden adds salt to the wounds of unemployment.
Some, including the NITI report, have suggested linking education to skills that will make youth more employable, but it cannot by itself create demand for their labor. India, therefore, also needs faster creation of productive, reasonably secure jobs capable of absorbing a large and increasingly educated workforce.
There is another problem—the informal sector is massive. Another paper published by NITI in March estimates that only 23 percent of India’s workforce are regular wage/salaried employees, while 19 percent are casual workers. The rest—about 58 percent—are self-employed/micro-entrepreneurs. Here, ‘self-employment’ often masks underemployment rather than genuine entrepreneurship.
Besides, the credibility of government data on unemployment has been called into question. A 2025 Reuters poll revealed that most of the independent economists who participated in the survey believed the Indian government’s unemployment data masks the severity of joblessness and underemployment. Official surveys use outdated definitions — counting anyone who works for as little as one hour per week as employed, they pointed out.
This means that India’s unemployment crisis is bigger than what it appears to be.
Economists have proposed various solutions. Raising concerns about the impact of automation and AI on future employment, development economist Santosh Mehrotra has called for a stronger manufacturing strategy. Former Reserve Bank of India chief Raghuram Rajan said India needed “structural economic pivots toward labor-intensive white-collar and specialized job creation.” Many have urged shifting focus away from purely capital-heavy incentives toward sectors like textiles, leather, and light engineering that can absorb the millions moving away from agriculture.
Such proposals would require policy reversals by the Narendra Modi government. Whether the government aims for such changes to earn the confidence of the youth remains to be seen.

articles.title: Philippine Peso Slumps to Record Low Amid Rising Energy Prices
articles.full_text:
Like some of its regional counterparts, the Philippines continues to be buffeted by the economic shocks of the U.S.-Iran war.
The Philippine peso fell to a record low on Friday due to rising oil prices and a strengthening U.S. dollar, despite attempts by the country’s central bank to offer relief.
According to a report by Inquirer.net, which cited data from Bankers Association of the Philippines, the currency weakened 37.7 centavos to close at 62.265 per U.S. dollar, surpassing the previous record-low close of 61.888 set the day prior.
The new record capped off three straight weeks of losses for the peso, which has been among the Asian currencies most vulnerable to the spike in energy prices brought about by the war in the Middle East. The peso has lost nearly 8 percent since the Iran war began on February 28, due in large part to the Philippines’ heavy reliance on oil imports, which has contributed to rising inflation.
This came despite a decision by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas to raise its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points point to 5 percent. Central bank Governor Eli Remolona Jr. described the increase, which brought the total increase in the current anti-inflation campaign to 75 basis points, as a “preemptive” move against emerging inflation risks. Philippine policymakers now expect inflation to average 6.1 percent this year, and 5.4 percent in 2027, up from a decade-long low of 1.7 percent in 2025 and 3.2 percent in 2024.
Citi analysts told Reuters that the outlook for the currency remained negative, “due to significant external pressures.”
“The current-account deficit is widening, driven by elevated energy prices and a weaker services balance in the recent quarter,” the analysts stated. “This pressure could persist, as future government infrastructure spending would keep the import bill elevated.”
Among Asian currencies, the other major casualty of the Iran war has been the Indonesian rupiah, which fell by around 8 percent in the first six months of 2026, and in early June sunk to a record low of 18,190 against the dollar – lower than even during the depths of the Asian financial crisis of 1997-1998.
The currency has been under pressure since President Prabowo Subianto came to office in October 2024, promising high-spending social programs that sent a tremor of concern through the markets. However, these concerns have only bene compounded by the economic reverberations of the Iran war.
The Thai baht has also weakened, falling to 32.96 to the U.S. dollar at the close of its last session, down 4.6 percent since the start of 2026.
The immediate impacts of the weak peso are likely to be mixed. As Inquirer.net reported, millions of families will benefit from the fact that remittances from relatives abroad will be worth more locally, potentially giving households greater spending power. Exporters may also benefit as a weaker currency makes Philippine goods more competitive overseas.
However, it noted that a weaker peso “also raises the cost of imported goods, while companies and the government face higher peso costs when repaying foreign-currency debt.”

Among Asian currencies, the other major casualty of the Iran war has been the Indonesian rupiah, which fell by around 8 percent in the first six months of 2026, and in early June sunk to a record low of 18,190 against the dollar – lower than even during the depths of the Asian financial crisis of 1997-1998.
The currency has been under pressure since President Prabowo Subianto came to office in October 2024, promising high-spending social programs that sent a tremor of concern through the markets. However, these concerns have only bene compounded by the economic reverberations of the Iran war.
The Thai baht has also weakened, falling to 32.96 to the U.S. dollar at the close of its last session, down 4.6 percent since the start of 2026.
The immediate impacts of the weak peso are likely to be mixed. As Inquirer.net reported, millions of families will benefit from the fact that remittances from relatives abroad will be worth more locally, potentially giving households greater spending power. Exporters may also benefit as a weaker currency makes Philippine goods more competitive overseas.
However, it noted that a weaker peso “also raises the cost of imported goods, while companies and the government face higher peso costs when repaying foreign-currency debt.”
The Philippine peso fell to a record low on Friday due to rising oil prices and a strengthening U.S. dollar, despite attempts by the country’s central bank to offer relief.
According to a report by Inquirer.net, which cited data from Bankers Association of the Philippines, the currency weakened 37.7 centavos to close at 62.265 per U.S. dollar, surpassing the previous record-low close of 61.888 set the day prior.
Sebastian Strangio is Southeast Asia editor at The Diplomat.
articles.summary: Like some of its regional counterparts, the Philippines continues to be buffeted by the economic shocks of the U.S.-Iran war.
